questions.q: In which direction does heat always flow between two objects of different temperatures?
questions.a: Heat always flows from the hotter object to the cooler object. A student who says it flows from "cold to hot" is confusing the sensation of feeling cold (losing heat) with the actual movement of energy.

questions.q: If you hold an ice cube in your hand, why does your hand feel cold?
questions.a: Your hand feels cold because heat is flowing out of your hand and into the ice cube. A student who says "the cold moves into my hand" is misinterpreting the direction of energy transfer; cold is simply the absence of heat.

questions.q: A metal rod is held over a candle flame. After a few minutes, the other end becomes hot. What is this mode of heat transfer called?
questions.a: This is called conduction. If the student answers "convection," they are likely confusing how solids transfer heat versus how liquids/gases move heat via currents.

questions.q: Compare the way a room is warmed by a heater (convection) and the way the Sun warms the Earth (radiation). Why is there a difference?
questions.a: The heater warms the air, which moves in currents (convection), whereas the Sun’s heat travels through space where there is no air (radiation). A student struggling here might not realize that radiation does not require a medium to travel, while convection requires air or liquid to circulate.

questions.q: Why is it impossible for heat to spontaneously flow from a cold block of ice to a hot cup of coffee?
questions.a: This violates the fundamental rule of physics that energy flows from higher intensity (hot) to lower intensity (cold). Claiming it could flow the other way suggests a misunderstanding of the nature of energy equilibrium.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment to prove that heat flows through metal faster than through wood.
questions.a: A good answer involves placing a metal spoon and a wooden spoon of the same size into a mug of hot water and touching the handles after two minutes. A poor answer fails to control variables (e.g., using different sized spoons) or doesn't mention the "hot water" source.
